Reports & interpretation · 5 MIN READ

How to read a laboratory report with confidence

Understand identifiers, reported units, observations and the scope of findings.

KNOWLEDGE & INSIGHTS

Ideas for interpreting the questions behind materials and laboratory reports.

← Back to insights

Understand identifiers, reported units, observations and the scope of findings.

Find the specimen identity first

A report should be read against the exact sample or item it describes. Check identifiers, piece counts, material form and any relevant dates or references before interpreting a number or conclusion.

Where there are several samples, matching each result to the correct specimen is essential. A result for one stone or test portion does not automatically describe other materials supplied at the same time.

Read units and context together

Percent, parts per million, mass fractions and fineness conventions describe different quantities. Confirm which unit applies and whether values describe a measured concentration, an observation or an interpreted classification.

Methods have intended applications and limitations. Technical notes, reporting thresholds, sample preparation details and uncertainty information—when supplied—give context that a single result alone does not convey.

Avoid conclusions beyond the report

A reported property is not automatically a statement of market value, regulatory compliance or geological provenance. Those wider conclusions may require other records, methods or professional assessments.

When a term is unclear, ask which specimen and method it refers to and what can reasonably be inferred. A sound report supports informed questions as well as informed decisions.
